summary.text: Nuclear fusion is a reaction in which two or more atomic nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus.
The difference in mass between what goes in and what comes out shows up as released or absorbed energy, and active stellar cores are powered by fusion.
Fusion typically needs very high temperature, density and confinement time, and fusion power research seeks to use it for energy.

paragraphs.heading: Joining nuclei together
paragraphs.text: In nuclear fusion, two or more atomic nuclei merge into one larger nucleus. What comes out does not have quite the same mass as what went in, and that gap in mass shows up as energy, either given off or taken in. The gap exists because the nuclear binding energy of the nuclei is different before and after the reaction.

paragraphs.heading: The engine of the stars
paragraphs.text: Fusion is what powers the cores of active stars. Fusion in stars, and in the Big Bang, built every element lighter than nickel, which has atomic number 28. Making nuclei lighter than nickel-62 by fusion normally gives off energy. The easiest nuclei to fuse are among the lightest, above all deuterium, tritium and helium-3. Nuclear fission, the opposite process, releases the most energy with very heavy nuclei, especially the actinides.

paragraphs.heading: What it takes
paragraphs.text: Fusion usually happens as thermonuclear fusion, which needs three things at once: a very high temperature, in the range of a hundred million kelvin, plus density and confinement time. Those conditions occur only in thermonuclear weapons, boosted fission weapons and fusion power experiments. Fusion power research aims to use the reaction to produce energy, and in magnetic confinement research the leading designs are tokamaks and stellarators. Fusion devices can also serve as sources of neutrons and help produce superheavy elements.

paragraphs.heading: Explaining the Sun
paragraphs.text: The American chemist William Draper Harkins was the first to suggest nuclear fusion, in 1915. In 1919 Francis William Aston invented the mass spectrometer, which revealed that four hydrogen atoms weigh more than one helium atom. From that, Arthur Eddington predicted correctly in 1920 that fusing hydrogen into helium could be the main source of a star's energy.

paragraphs.heading: Working out the details
paragraphs.text: In 1927 Friedrich Hund discovered quantum tunneling, in connection with electron levels. The next year George Gamow became the first to use tunneling for the nucleus, applying it to alpha decay and then to fusion as its reverse. Building on this, Robert Atkinson and Fritz Houtermans made the first estimates of fusion rates in stars in 1929. In 1938 Hans Bethe and Charles Critchfield set out the proton–proton chain that dominates in stars like the Sun, and in 1939 Bethe published the CNO cycle, common in heavier stars.

paragraphs.heading: From the lab to the bomb
paragraphs.text: At the Cavendish Laboratory, Mark Oliphant, Paul Harteck and Ernest Rutherford published, in May 1934, a deliberate deuterium fusion experiment, discovering both tritium and helium-3 along the way. It is widely seen as the first experimental demonstration of fusion. Research into fusion for weapons began in the early 1940s within the Manhattan Project. A full test of the Teller-Ulam design followed in the Ivy Mike test of November 1952, a two-stage device fusing liquid deuterium that yielded over 10 megatons of TNT equivalent.
